title: Male Pelvis & Perineum Anatomy: Viscera & Pelvic Floors
description: Explore male pelvis and perineum anatomy in sagittal and regional views, covering the bladder neck, prostate, rectum, levator ani floor, and perineal sacs.
h1: Male Pelvis and Perineum Anatomy: Pelvic Floor, Viscera and Pouches
blurb: Sagittal and perineal views of the male pelvis: bladder neck, walnut-sized prostate, rectum, levator ani muscular sling, and pudendal neurovascular canals.
lead: Within the bony ring of the male pelvis, the urinary bladder, prostate, and rectum share a compact muscular floor that supports abdominal viscera and controls continence. In this illustrated guide to male pelvis and perineum anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including urinary bladder, prostate gland, prostatic & membranous urethra, ejaculatory ducts—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Within the bony ring of the male pelvis, the urinary bladder, prostate, and rectum share a compact muscular floor that supports abdominal viscera and controls continence. Deep regional anatomy — the pouches, sphincters and nerves examined in every pelvic module. Within the human body, the male pelvis & perineum (Pelvis masculina) is situated in pelvic sagittal section, receives arterial perfusion via internal iliac branches, and is innervated by pudendal + pelvic splanchnics.

Structurally, the urinary bladder (Vesica urinaria) comprises reservoir behind the pubis. Physiologically, the urinary bladder stores urine; trigone is its smooth base. Structurally, the prostate gland (Glandula prostatica) comprises walnut gland around the prostatic urethra. Physiologically, the prostate gland governs seminal fluid (PSA, citric acid, fibrinolysin). Structurally, the prostatic & membranous urethra (Urethra masculina) comprises urethra traversing prostate and perineum. Physiologically, the prostatic & membranous urethra governs conduit for urine and semen; sphincters here. Structurally, the ejaculatory ducts (Ductus ejaculatorii) comprises vas + seminal vesicle ducts through prostate. Physiologically, the ejaculatory ducts deliver sperm into prostatic urethra. Structurally, the rectum comprises terminal 12–15 cm with three valves. Physiologically, the rectum stores stool before defecation. Structurally, the anal canal & sphincters (Canalis analis) comprises internal (smooth) + external (striated) sphincters. Physiologically, the anal canal & sphincters governs continence control.

Clinically, regarding the urinary bladder, outlet obstruction in men is usually prostatic. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the prostate gland, BPH compresses the urethra — hesitancy and nocturia. In clinical pathology involving the prostatic & membranous urethra, catheterisation respects the puboprostatic curve. Medical evaluation of the ejaculatory ducts also notes that obstruction → low-volume ejaculate.

questions.question: Which organs are located in the male pelvis?
questions.answer: The male pelvis contains bladder, prostate and rectum, along with parts of the urethra, reproductive ducts, pelvic vessels and nerves.

questions.question: What is the pelvic floor's role in men?
questions.answer: Pelvic-floor muscles support pelvic organs and contribute to continence. Their relationship to the urethra and perineal structures is important in regional anatomy.

questions.question: Where is the urinary bladder in the male pelvis?
questions.answer: In the male pelvis, the bladder lies superior to the prostate; the prostatic urethra begins at the bladder neck.

questions.question: Where are the prostatic and membranous urethral segments?
questions.answer: The prostatic urethra passes through the prostate; the membranous urethra continues through the pelvic floor and perineal membrane.

questions.question: What is the function of the rectum?
questions.answer: The rectum temporarily stores feces before defecation and empties into the anal canal.
